claim: Long-range material transport is essential to maintain the physiological functions of multicellular organisms such as animals and plants.
source: Long-range material transport is essential to maintain the physiological functions of multicellular organisms such as animals and plants.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about multicellular organisms.

claim: Material transport in bacteria is often short-ranged and limited by diffusion.
source: By contrast, material transport in bacteria is often short-ranged and limited by diffusion.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific understanding of bacterial material transport.

claim: A large-scale and temporally evolving open-channel system spontaneously develops in Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonies via shear-induced banding.
source: Using Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonies as a model system, we discover that a large-scale and temporally evolving open-channel system spontaneously develops in the colony via shear-induced banding.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental observations and data.

claim: Fluid flows in the open channels support high-speed transport of cells and outer membrane vesicles up to 450 µm/s over centimeters.
source: Fluid flows in the open channels support high-speed (up to 450 µm/s) transport of cells and outer membrane vesicles over centimeters
evidence: This is supported by direct experimental measurements of flow speeds in the study.

claim: The open channels help to eradicate colonies of a competing species Staphylococcus aureus.
source: Fluid flows in the open channels support high-speed (up to 450 µm/s) transport of cells and outer membrane vesicles over centimeters, and help to eradicate colonies of a competing species Staphylococcus aureus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from co-culture experiments.

claim: The channel flows are driven by interfacial tension mediated by cell-secreted biosurfactants.
source: the channel flows are driven by interfacial tension mediated by cell-secreted biosurfactants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental manipulations with rhamnolipids and mathematical modeling.

claim: Mechanochemical coupling between interfacial force and biosurfactant kinetics can coordinate large-scale material transport in primitive life forms.
source: Our findings demonstrate that mechanochemical coupling between interfacial force and biosurfactant kinetics can coordinate large-scale material transport in primitive life forms
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and modeling results.

claim: Hydraulic pressure due to active pumping drives the circulation of body fluid in blood and lymph vessel systems of animals.
source: For example, hydraulic pressure due to active pumping drives the circulation of body fluid in blood and lymph vessel systems of animals (Scallan et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Transpiration and capillary pressure passively drive the water transport through vascular tissues of plants.
source: transpiration and capillary pressure passively drive the water transport through vascular tissues of plants (Sack and Holbrook, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cilia beating of epithelial cells drives the cerebrospinal fluid flow in brain ventricles.
source: cilia beating of epithelial cells drives the cerebrospinal fluid flow in brain ventricles (Faubel et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cilia beating of epithelial cells drives mucus flow in the respiratory tract.
source: cilia beating of epithelial cells drives the cerebrospinal fluid flow in brain ventricles (Faubel et al., 2016) as well as mucus flow in the respiratory tract (Huang and Choma, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: At the single-cell level, diffusion governs nutrient uptake and sets a fundamental limit on the size of bacterial cells.
source: At the single-cell level, diffusion governs nutrient uptake and sets a fundamental limit on the size of bacterial cells (Berg, 1993; Nelson, 2003; Schulz and Jorgensen, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Diffusion has been assumed to dominate material transport in bacterial communities.
source: In bacterial communities, diffusion has been assumed to dominate material transport (Lavrentovich et al., 2013; Pirt, 1967; Shao et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Long-range directed material transport is deemed unusual in bacterial communities.
source: long-range directed material transport is deemed unusual, despite the notion that bacterial communities resemble multicellular organisms in many aspects such as coordinated metabolism, communication, and division of labor (Lee et al., 2017; Parsek and Greenberg, 2005; Shapiro, 1998; van Gestel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and established knowledge.

claim: Long-range flows were driven by flagellar motility in sediment biofilms.
source: Among these examples, it was shown that long-range flows were driven by flagellar motility in sediment biofilms (Fenchel and Glud, 1998; Petroff and Libchaber, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Long-range flows were driven by flagellar motility in bacterial colonies.
source: it was shown that long-range flows were driven by flagellar motility in sediment biofilms (Fenchel and Glud, 1998; Petroff and Libchaber, 2014) and in bacterial colonies (Wu et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Directed transport can be driven by passive forces such as osmosis and evaporation-induced pressure gradient with a speed of ~0.1–10 µm/s.
source: directed transport can also be driven by passive forces such as osmosis and evaporation-induced pressure gradient (Wilking et al., 2013; Wu and Berg, 2012), with a speed of ~0.1–10 µm/s.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Intra-colony channel structures have been identified in a few bacterial species.
source: Intra-colony channel structures have been identified in a few bacterial species (Davey et al., 2003; Drury et al., 1993; Rooney et al., 2020; Stoodley et al., 1994; Xu et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previously identified channel structures have a typical persistence length of a few micron to tens of microns, thus not able to support directed transport beyond millimeter scale.
source: these channel structures have a typical persistence length of a few micron to tens of microns, thus not able to support directed transport beyond millimeter scale.
evidence: This is based on citations to prior work and logical inference about transport capabilities.

claim: Many bacterial species synthesize biosurfactants in a tightly regulated manner.
source: For bacterial communities, interfacial tension may potentially offer such a driving force because many bacterial species synthesize biosurfactants (i.e., surface active agents that reduce interfacial energy or surface tension Chandler, 1987) in a tightly regulated manner (Ron and Rosenberg, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Colonies of wildtype and pilB-knockout mutant P. aeruginosa displayed rapid cellular flows streaming through the interior of the colonies.
source: In the colonies of wildtype and pilB-knockout mutant (PA14 ΔpilB; denoted as non-piliated mutant), we were intrigued to observe rapid cellular flows streaming through the interior of the colonies, while there was little collective directed motion on both sides of the streams (Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments.

claim: The streams in wildtype and pilB-knockout mutant colonies were tens of microns in width and up to millimeters in length.
source: The streams were tens of microns in width and up to millimeters in length
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental observations.

claim: The courses of streams in wildtype and pilB-knockout mutant colonies were highly unstable presumably due to continuous disruption by cellular motion driven by flagellar motility.
source: but their courses were highly unstable presumably due to continuous disruption by cellular motion driven by flagellar motility.
evidence: This is an observation with a speculative explanation.

claim: Non-motile and piliated P. aeruginosa colonies presented many low-cell-density valleys extending from colony center to the edge over centimeters with high directional persistence.
source: On the other hand, for PA14 mutants without flagellar motility, namely, PA14 flgK::Tn5 ΔpilA (with both flagellar motility and type IV pilus-mediated motility disabled; denoted by 'non-motile P. aeruginosa') (Beaussart et al., 2014) and PA14 flgK::Tn5 (without flagellar motility but with functional type IV pilus-mediated motility; denoted by 'piliated P. aeruginosa') (Lee et al., 2011; 'Methods'), we observed by naked eyes that the colonies of both strains presented many low-cell-density valleys extending from colony center to the edge over centimeters with high directional persistence (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments shown in figures.

claim: The centimeter-long valleys in non-motile and piliated P. aeruginosa colonies were fluid-filled, free-surface channels ~5–10 µm in height and tens to several hundred µm in width.
source: Under the microscope, we found that these remarkable, centimeter-long valleys were fluid-filled, free-surface channels (i.e., open channels) ~5–10 µm in height and tens to several hundred µm in width
evidence: This is a measurement from microscopy observations.

claim: Cells carried by the fluid flow in canals streamed rapidly at speeds up to hundreds of µm/s in coherent directions.
source: in which cells carried by the fluid flow streamed rapidly at speeds up to hundreds of µm/s in coherent directions (Figure 1E, Appendix 1—figure 1A, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental observations shown in figures and videos.

claim: The fluid flow in channels on average went towards the colony edge and stopped abruptly at the very end of a channel.
source: The fluid flow in channels on average went towards the colony edge and stopped abruptly at the very end (i.e., the tip) of a channel, disappearing into the dense layer of cells near the edge (Appendix 1—figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments.

claim: The fluid flow in canals was sensitive to water content in the air environment and was easily disrupted by decrease of humidity.
source: The fluid flow was sensitive to water content in the air environment, and it was easily disrupted by decrease of humidity.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments.

claim: Nearby channels could merge with each other while individual channels could split, resulting in a large-scale channel network across the entire colony.
source: Nearby channels could merge with each other while individual channels could split, resulting in a large-scale channel network across the entire colony (Figure 1B and D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments shown in figures.

claim: The large-scale open channels have a free upper surface and are distinct from the pipe-like closed channels or conduits previously reported in bacterial colonies.
source: These large-scale open channels have a free upper surface, and therefore, they are distinct from the pipe-like closed channels or conduits previously reported in bacterial colonies (Drury et al., 1993; Rooney et al., 2020; Stoodley et al., 1994; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work supported by citations and experimental observations.

claim: When the amount of surface water on agar plates was reduced by extended drying, piliated P. aeruginosa colonies displayed a unique branching morphology presumably driven by fingering instability.
source: When the amount of surface water on agar plates was reduced by extended drying ('Methods'), the piliated P. aeruginosa (PA14 flgK::Tn5) colonies displayed a unique branching morphology presumably driven by fingering instability in the presence of surface tension gradient in the colony (Trinschek et al., 2018; Troian et al., 1989; Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an observation with a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Each branch in branching colonies hosted a single canal that ran through the entire branch.
source: Interestingly each branch was highly directed and hosted a single canal that ran through the entire branch (Figure 1F, Figure 1—video 2; Appendix 1—figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments shown in figures and videos.

claim: The emergence of canals in branching colonies occurred robustly at ~8 hr at 30°C or ~15 hr at room temperature after inoculation.
source: The emergence of canals in such branching colonies occurred robustly at ~8 hr (at 30°C) or ~15 hr (at room temperature) after inoculation.
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental observations.

claim: The rhamnolipid-deficient mutant PA14 flgK::Tn5 ΔrhlA was unable to develop canals.
source: We found that this rhamnolipid-deficient mutant (PA14 flgK::Tn5 ΔrhlA) was unable to develop canals (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments with a genetic mutant.

claim: The rhamnolipid-deficient mutant colony showed no sign of any mesoscale flows under the microscope.
source: also the colony showed no sign of any mesoscale flows under the microscope.
evidence: This is a direct observation from microscopy.

claim: Artificial surface tension gradient established by injecting exogenous rhamnolipids restored canal formation in colonies of the rhamnolipid-deficient mutant.
source: Next, to show that Marangoni stress could drive canal formation, we established artificial surface tension gradient in colonies by injecting an exogenous source of rhamnolipids via a programmable syringe pump ('Methods'), and it restored canal formation in colonies of the rhamnolipid-deficient mutant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result demonstrating causation.

claim: The height of agar under canals and other regions of the colony was uniform and there was no sign of agar degradation.
source: We found that while the colony thickness above agar had an abrupt drop near canals, the height of agar under canals and other regions of the colony was uniform and there was no sign of agar degradation (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a measurement from laser scanning confocal microscopy.

claim: Canal development requires rhamnolipids but not agar degradation.
source: Taken together, these results show that canal development requires rhamnolipids but not agar degradation
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: Fluid flows in canals are driven by rhamnolipids-mediated surface tension gradient.
source: and they provide strong evidence that fluid flows in canals are driven by rhamnolipids-mediated surface tension gradient.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: When a counteracting surface tension gradient was applied by placing an agar patch containing surfactant Tween 20 in front of a colony branch, fluid flows in the canal gradually ceased and the canal slowly retracted.
source: When we applied a counteracting surface tension gradient directing toward the colony center by placing an agar patch containing surfactant Tween 20 (50 mg/mL, surface tension ~4 × 10-2 N/m) ~1 cm in front of a colony branch, fluid flows in the canal gradually ceased and the canal (but not the colony branch) slowly retracted (Video 2; 'Methods')
evidence: This is a direct experimental result shown in a video.

claim: The driving force of canal flows is comparable in magnitude to that provided by a surface tension gradient of ~ 103 mN·m–2.
source: suggesting that the driving force of canal flows is comparable in magnitude to that provided by a surface tension gradient of ~ 103 mN·m–2.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental result with Tween 20.

claim: The rhlA promoter activity was azimuthally symmetric in early-stage colonies and the overall PrhlA-gfp(ASV) fluorescence increased monotonically until canals emerged.
source: we found that the rhlA promoter activity was azimuthally symmetric in early-stage colonies and the overall PrhlA-gfp(ASV) fluorescence increased monotonically until canals emerged (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is a measurement from fluorescence reporter experiments shown in figures.

claim: Rhamnolipids in the colony center were continuously synthesized, thus generating a radial gradient of surface tension.
source: The result shows that rhamnolipids in the colony center were continuously synthesized, thus generating a radial gradient of surface tension.
evidence: This is an inference from the fluorescence reporter data.

claim: The flow speed profile in regions with homogeneous cell density distribution displayed flow regimes with distinct shear rates.
source: Flow speed measurement by particle image velocimetry (PIV) analysis ('Methods') in colonies before canals became visible to naked eyes revealed that the flow speed profile in regions with homogeneous cell density distribution displayed flow regimes with distinct shear rates (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—video 1; 'Methods').
evidence: This is a measurement from PIV analysis shown in figures.

claim: As time went by, fluid flows in the high shear domains carried away cells in nearby areas, and the course got widened and gradually became fixed canals.
source: as time went by, fluid flows in the high shear domains carried away cells in nearby areas, and the course got widened and gradually became fixed canals (Figure 3C, 32–56 min, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in figures and videos.

claim: The presence of distinct flow regimes under presumably uniform shear stress and the instability of flow courses are hallmarks of shear-induced banding.
source: The presence of distinct flow regimes under presumably uniform shear stress (Figure 3A and B) and the instability of flow courses (Figure 3C) are hallmarks of shear-induced banding, a phenomenon often seen in complex fluids (Divoux et al., 2016; Olmsted, 2008; Ovarlez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental observations supported by citations to prior work on complex fluids.

claim: Canals emerge via the onset of shear-induced banding in the colony fluids.
source: These results suggest that canals emerge via the onset of shear-induced banding in the colony fluids (see more in 'Discussion').
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations and comparison with complex fluid behavior.

claim: The time-averaged peak cell speed near the center of canals was ~200 µm/s with transient speeds up to 450 µm/s.
source: We found that the time-averaged peak cell speed near the center of canals was ~200 µm/s (with transient speeds up to 450 µm/s) (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is a measurement from cell tracking experiments shown in figures.

claim: The peak flow speed in canals was higher than other reported forms of bacterial long-range directed transport and most forms of active bacterial motility.
source: higher than other reported forms of bacterial long-range directed transport (Fenchel and Glud, 1998; Petroff and Libchaber, 2014; Wilking et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2019) and most forms of active bacterial motility (Mitchell and Kogure, 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work supported by citations.

claim: There was a high-flow-speed region spanning ~20 mm from the canal tip toward the colony center, and the flow speed diminished further toward the colony center.
source: As shown by the plateau in Figure 3E, we found a high-flow-speed region spanning ~20 mm from the canal tip toward the colony center, and the flow speed diminished further toward the colony center.
evidence: This is a measurement from flow speed profiling shown in figures.

claim: The surface tension near the colony center has decreased to a steady-state level, presumably due to the saturated concentrations of rhamnolipids there.
source: This result reveals the spatial distribution of Marangoni stress and suggests that the surface tension near the colony center has decreased to a steady-state level, presumably due to the saturated concentrations of rhamnolipids there.
evidence: This is an inference from the flow speed measurements with a speculative explanation.

claim: The Marangoni stress in canals was on the order of ~1000 mN·m–2 in order to support a peak flow speed of ~400 µm/s.
source: First of all, we used finite-element simulation of Navier–Stokes equation in a simplified canal geometry (Figure 4A; 'Methods') to estimate that the Marangoni stress in canals was on the order of ~1000 mN·m–2 in order to support a peak flow speed of ~400 µm/s.
evidence: This is an estimate from numerical simulation.

claim: The magnitude of Marangoni stress roughly corresponds to the surface tension gradient established between a saturated source of rhamnolipids and a surfactant-free region over a distance of ~4 cm.
source: This magnitude roughly corresponds to the surface tension gradient established between a saturated source of rhamnolipids (surface tension ~30 mN/m; Appendix 1—figure 3) and a surfactant-free region (surface tension ~70 mN/m; Appendix 1—figure 3) over a distance of ~4 cm
evidence: This is a calculation based on measured surface tension values and geometric considerations.

claim: The distribution of interface-associated surfactant displayed a saturated region near the colony center followed by a biphasic decrease toward the spreading front of the colony.
source: As shown by the numerical simulation results based on the model, the distribution of interface-associated surfactant displayed a saturated region near the colony center (Figure 4D) (corresponding to the region with minimal surface tension in Appendix 1—figure 4A), followed by a biphasic decrease toward the spreading front of the colony (corresponding to the increase of surface tension in Appendix 1—figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling.

claim: The resultant surface tension gradient was nearly zero near the colony center, which agrees with the experimental result.
source: The resultant surface tension gradient (and therefore flow speed) was nearly zero near the colony center, which agrees with the experimental result (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is a comparison between modeling results and experimental data.

claim: The surface tension gradient displayed a pronounced plateau with modest inclination, which is in qualitative agreement with the measured flow speed profile in canals.
source: further away from the center, it displayed a pronounced plateau (i.e., ranging from the peak to knee of each curve at specific time points, corresponding to the region with rapid canal flows) with modest inclination (Figure 4E). These results are in qualitative agreement with the measured flow speed profile in canals (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is a comparison between modeling results and experimental data.

claim: The entire plateau of surface tension gradient moves away from colony center at a speed of ~1 mm/hr, with the width increasing gradually from ~20 mm to ~30 mm in 15 hr while the height decreasing by ~20%.
source: More importantly, our simulation results were able to reveal that the entire plateau moves away from colony center at a speed of ~1 mm/hr, with the width increasing gradually from ~20 mm to ~30 mm in 15 hr while the height decreasing by ~20% (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling shown in figures.

claim: The high-speed directed flows at a specific location in the canal can persist for ~20–30 hr.
source: Consequently, the high-speed directed flows at a specific location in the canal can persist for ~20–30 hr.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Fluorescently labeled OMVs with a mean size of ~150 nm were transported along the canal over centimeter distances with a peak speed of >200 μm/s.
source: We found that these OMVs, having a mean size of ~150 nm (Appendix 1—figure 5), were transported along the canal over centimeter distances (Figure 5A–C) with a peak speed of >200 μm/s (Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from OMV tracking experiments shown in figures and videos.

claim: S. aureus colonies irrigated by canal flows were quickly eradicated, with <2% of the initial cell mass remaining after 60 min of contact with canal flows.
source: We found that S. aureus colonies irrigated by canal flows were quickly eradicated (Figure 5D, Figure 5—video 2; Appendix 1—figure 6), with <2% of the initial cell mass remaining after 60 min of contact with canal flows (Figure 5E, curve labeled as 'irrigated').
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from co-culture experiments shown in figures and videos.

claim: S. aureus colonies that were in contact with P. aeruginosa colony but did not encounter canal flows retained ~40% of the initial cell mass after 60 min of contact.
source: By contrast, S. aureus colonies that were in contact with P. aeruginosa colony but did not encounter canal flows retained ~40% of the initial cell mass after 60 min of contact (Figure 5E, curve labeled as 'non-irrigated').
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from co-culture experiments shown in figures.

claim: Fluid flows in canals help to eradicate competing bacterial species.
source: These results demonstrated that fluid flows in canals help to eradicate competing bacterial species.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-culture experimental results.

claim: Canal flows may increase the flux of P. aeruginosa-produced antimicrobial substances and therefore enhance the efficiency of inhibiting competing bacterial species.
source: We suggest that canal flows may increase the flux of P. aeruginosa-produced antimicrobial substances, such as quinolines encapsulated in OMVs with antibacterial activities against Gram-positive bacteria (Mashburn and Whiteley, 2005) and toxic compounds carried by rhamnolipid micelles (Gdaniec et al., 2022), and therefore enhance the efficiency of inhibiting competing bacterial species.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The rapid eradication of S. aureus colonies was most likely due to substances encapsulated in OMVs and rhamnolipid micelles that were transported by canals.
source: Therefore, the rapid eradication of S. aureus colonies was most likely due to substances encapsulated in OMVs (Mashburn and Whiteley, 2005) and rhamnolipid micelles (Gdaniec et al., 2022) that were transported by canals.
evidence: This is an inference from experimental results and prior knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Wildtype P. aeruginosa colonies displayed rapid streams within the colony but the streams did not turn into stable and persistent canals.
source: Indeed, wildtype P. aeruginosa colonies displayed rapid streams within the colony but the streams did not turn into stable and persistent canals (Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from experiments shown in a video.

claim: Flagellar motility weakens cell–cell adhesion and disrupts the course of high-shear flow regimes, thus preventing the high-shear flow regimes from further developing into more stable courses or canals.
source: Flagellar motility weakens cell–cell adhesion and disrupts the course of high-shear flow regimes, thus preventing the high-shear flow regimes from further developing into more stable courses or canals.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed instability.

claim: P. aeruginosa cells tend to downregulate flagellar motility in the airways of patients with CF.
source: Although P. aeruginosa cells tend to downregulate flagellar motility in the airways of patients with CF (Luzar et al., 1985; Mahenthiralingam et al., 1994; Wolfgang et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Serratia marcescens is able to develop canal-like structures during swarming, but such structures are only found at the center of the colony where most cells appear to be sessile.
source: We note that another flagellated and biosurfactant-producing bacteria Serratia marcescens is able to develop canal-like structures during swarming (Appendix 1—figure 7), but such structures are only found at the center of the colony where most cells appear to be sessile.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments shown in appendix figures.

claim: Colony expansion normally does not lead to directed transport of materials within the colony.
source: Colony expansion normally does not lead to directed transport of materials within the colony.
evidence: This is a general statement based on understanding of colony dynamics.

claim: During swarming of wildtype P. aeruginosa facilitated by Marangoni stress, the colony expansion speed was ~1 µm/s, which is one order of magnitude slower than individual cells' random motion.
source: For example, during swarming of wildtype P. aeruginosa facilitated by Marangoni stress, the colony expansion speed was ~1 µm/s (Fauvart et al., 2012), which is one order of magnitude slower than individual cells' random motion (tens of µm/s)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and comparison with known cell motility speeds.

claim: Directed material transport within a colony does not necessarily coincide with colony expansion, and the speed of the two processes could differ by orders of magnitude.
source: Moreover, as demonstrated in this study, directed material transport within a colony does not necessarily coincide with colony expansion (e.g., see Appendix 1—figure 1—video 2), and the speed of the two processes could differ by orders of magnitude (~200 µm/s versus ~2 mm/hr).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations shown in videos.

claim: The cross-sectional flow velocity profile of a mixture of dense bacterial suspension and concentrated rhamnolipids was highly asymmetric and signaled shear banding.
source: Under controlled flow conditions in PDMS microfluidic channels, we found that the cross-sectional flow velocity profile of a mixture of dense bacterial suspension (~1.35 × 1010 cells/mL) and concentrated rhamnolipids at 10 mg/mL, ~100 times critical miceller concentration (CMC) (Zhao et al., 2018) was highly asymmetric and signaled shear banding (Appendix 1—figure 8A)
evidence: This is a direct observation from microfluidic experiments shown in appendix figures.

claim: The flow velocity profile of pure cell suspension or of a mixture of rhamnolipids and dense microsphere suspension was closer to the parabolic profile characteristic of Newtonian fluids.
source: whereas the flow velocity profile of pure cell suspension at the same density or of a mixture of rhamnolipids (10 mg/mL) and dense 1.1 µm microsphere suspension (~1.9 × 1010 particles/mL) was closer to the parabolic profile characteristic of Newtonian fluids (Appendix 1—figure 8B and C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microfluidic experiments shown in appendix figures.

claim: The onset of shear banding in P. aeruginosa colonies preceding canal formation requires the interaction between cells and rhamnolipids.
source: This result suggests that the onset of shear banding in P. aeruginosa colonies preceding canal formation requires the interaction between cells and rhamnolipids (most likely in the form of micelles).
evidence: This is an inference from the microfluidic experimental results.

claim: Marangoni stress was previously suggested to contribute to the expansion of bacterial colonies.
source: Marangoni stress was previously suggested to contribute to the expansion of bacterial colonies (Angelini et al., 2009; Du et al., 2012; Fauvart et al., 2012; Rhodeland et al., 2020; Trinschek et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Canals develop robustly over a relatively wide range of agar concentration between 0.5% and 1.0% wt/vol.
source: We varied the agar concentration and found that canals develop robustly over a relatively wide range of agar concentration between 0.5% and 1.0% wt/vol (Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result shown in appendix figures.

claim: Above 1.0% agar concentration, canals were not observed presumably because the cells have difficulty to extract sufficient water to maintain an open-surface liquid film on the agar surface.
source: Above 1.0%, canals were not observed presumably because the cells have difficulty to extract sufficient water to maintain an open-surface liquid film on the agar surface, which is the same underlying reason why most bacteria cannot swarm on agar above 1.0% as swarming also requires maintaining open-surface liquid films (Kearns, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to prior work on swarming.

claim: The bacterial canals are reminiscent of human-made canals for cargo transport.
source: The open channels we found here are reminiscent of human-made canals for cargo transport, so we refer to these open channels as 'bacterial canals.'
evidence: This is an analogy drawn by the authors.

claim: P. aeruginosa produces outer membrane vesicles to deliver pathogenic factors, antimicrobial compounds, intercellular signals, and public goods.
source: P. aeruginosa produces OMVs to deliver pathogenic factors, antimicrobial compounds, intercellular signals, and public goods that either dissolve poorly or are prone to rapid dilution in the extracellular milieu (Bomberger et al., 2009; Mashburn and Whiteley, 2005; Schwechheimer and Kuehn, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: OMVs are slow in diffusion because their sizes are highly heterogeneous ranging from several tens to hundreds of nanometers.
source: OMVs are slow in diffusion because their sizes are highly heterogeneous ranging from several tens to hundreds of nanometers.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of diffusion and particle size.

claim: Imaging of P. aeruginosa aggregation patterns in situ in sputum samples from CF patients did not reveal canal-like structures.
source: Imaging of P. aeruginosa aggregation patterns in situ in sputum samples from CF patients did not reveal canal-like structures (DePas et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Canal formation may not occur in sputum samples from CF patients.
source: suggesting that canal formation may not occur in such conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited observation.

claim: The instability of streams in wildtype colonies was presumably caused by continuous displacement of cells driven by flagellar motility.
source: The instability was presumably caused by continuous displacement of cells driven by flagellar motility.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phenomenon.

claim: Cells translocating along the channels eventually settled in near the colony edge and they may contribute to colony expansion.
source: Cells translocating along the channels eventually settled in near the colony edge and they may contribute to colony expansion
evidence: This is an observation with a speculative interpretation.

claim: Channel formation does not necessarily coincide with colony expansion.
source: however, channel formation does not necessarily coincide with colony expansion (e.g., see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is stated as a finding with reference to further discussion.

claim: The colonies expanded at a steady-state speed of ~2 mm/hr at 30°C.
source: The colonies expanded at a steady-state speed of ~2 mm/hr at 30°C.
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental observations.

claim: The artificial surface tension gradient also promoted colony expansion.
source: We note that the artificial surface tension gradient also promoted colony expansion (Figure 2B), but again canal formation does not necessarily coincide with colony expansion (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is an observation from experiments shown in figures.

claim: The type IV pilus-mediated motility did not contribute to the movement of isolated cells being transported in canals since type IV pilus-mediated motility requires surface attachment and the resultant speed is only a few µm/s.
source: Note that the type IV pilus-mediated motility did not contribute to the movement of these isolated cells being transported in canals since type IV pilus-mediated motility requires surface attachment and the resultant speed is only a few µm/s (Talà et al., 2019)
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of type IV pilus motility supported by a citation.

claim: The movement of isolated cells in canals followed fluid motion in canals.
